assignment.title: Graphing Inequalities in Two Variables (M3 T2 L4)
assignment.essentialQuestion: What does the graph of a linear inequality in two variables look like? How does it compare to the graph of a linear equation?
assignment.instructions: Graphing inequalities in two variables. Every graph is built in the graphing workspace one step at a time — the boundary line, solid or dashed, the side to shade, and a test point — and each step is checked. For a word problem, write the inequality in the tool before you graph it. You have 3 tries on each Warm-Up, Classwork and Practice question, with hints. The Exit Ticket is one try with no hints.
assignment.teacherNotes: Algebra I Module 3 Topic 2 Lesson 4, from the district slides (two 45-minute days), TEKS A.2H and A.3D. Classwork order: Activity 4.2's first graph, y > 4x − 6 (CW 6), comes right after CW 1, before Kai's goal is graphed. Warm-Up rebuilt as readiness: a number-line solution statement (open/closed circle → dashed/solid), graphing the boundary line, and testing points. Every graph is built in the Systems Workspace's inequality builder (boundary, line style, shading, test point), and context items have students write the model in the tool first. Warm-Up and Exit Ticket are generated per student and back Recovery. Slide note: the worked example's title reads "Write a linear equality"; it means inequality.

sections.title: Warm-Up — From Number Lines to Half-Planes

questions.prompt: Making a statement. Graph the solution set of $x < {{a}}$ on the number line. Is {{a}} itself a solution? Your circle should say so.
directionSteps: Decide whether the circle is open or closed.
hints: An open circle means the number is not a solution; a closed circle means it is.
x < a is true for every number to the left of a on the number line.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. For x < 2, the number 2 is…

steps.title: Solution statements
steps.instruction: x = 2 is one point; x < 2 and x > 2 leave 2 out (open circle); x ≤ 2 and x ≥ 2 include it (closed circle).

steps.title: Coming up
steps.instruction: In two variables, the open circle becomes a dashed boundary line and the closed circle a solid one.

solutionReview.headline: Open circle at {{a}}, shaded to the left.
reasoning: < is strict, so {{a}} is not a solution: use an open circle.
Every number less than {{a}} is a solution, so shade to the left.
solutionReview.commonError: Using a closed circle: {{a}} < {{a}} is false, so {{a}} is not in the solution set.

questions.prompt: Graph {{equation}}. Plot its y-intercept, then use the slope to plot a second point. In this lesson a line like this becomes the boundary of an inequality.
directionSteps: Use the slope to plot a second point.
Draw the line through both points.
hints: The constant term is the y-intercept: plot that point on the y-axis first.
The slope is rise over run: from the y-intercept, move up (or down) and right.
Check your second point by substituting it into the equation.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. A slope of 3 means…

reasoning: Plot the y-intercept, (0, b).
Use the slope as rise over run to plot a second point.
Draw the line through both points.
solutionReview.commonError: Starting at the slope instead of the y-intercept.

questions.prompt: Test points. For $y \ge {{m|coef}}x {{b|signed}}$, find the value of the right side at each point's x-coordinate. Which point is a solution?
directionSteps: Decide which point makes the inequality true.
hints: Substitute the x-coordinate (and the y-coordinate) of each point.
A point is a solution when the inequality is a true statement there.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. A point is a solution of an inequality when, substituted, it makes the inequality…

solutionReview.headline: Compare each y-coordinate with the boundary’s value.
reasoning: At x = {{x1}} the right side is {{r1}}; at x = {{x2}} it is {{r2}}.
Only ({{xa}}, {{ya}}) has a y-coordinate at least as large as the right side.
solutionReview.commonError: Comparing the x-coordinate with the right side instead of the y-coordinate.

sections.title: Classwork — Graphing Linear Inequalities in Two Variables

questions.prompt: Activity 4.1 — Linear Inequalities in Two Variables. Coach Garcia is analyzing the scoring patterns of players on his basketball team. Kai averages 20 points per game from two-point and three-point shots. Let x be the number of two-point shots and y the number of three-point shots. Find Kai’s points for each game, and write an equation for every combination that totals exactly 20 points.
directionSteps: Find the points for each game.
Decide whether Kai meets the average.
Write the equation for exactly 20 points.

responses.label: 6 two-point shots and 2 three-point shots: total points
Does Kai meet her average in that game?
7 two-point shots and 2 three-point shots: total points
7 two-point shots and 4 three-point shots: total points

hints: A two-point shot is worth 2 points: multiply each count by its value.
Add the two products to get the total.
For the equation, set the total of the two kinds of shots equal to Kai’s average.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Points from x two-point shots is…

steps.title: Two variables
steps.instruction: One equation in two variables has many solutions: every pair (x, y) that makes it true. 2x + 3y = 20 is true for (7, 2), (10, 0), (4, 4) and more.

solutionReview.headline: Multiply each count by its point value, then add.
reasoning: 2(6) + 3(2) = 18, which is less than 20.
2(7) + 3(2) = 20 meets the average exactly; 2(7) + 3(4) = 26 is more than 20.
Every combination worth exactly 20 points satisfies 2x + 3y = 20.
solutionReview.commonError: Switching the point values: the two-point shots are x, so the term is 2x.

questions.prompt: Activity 4.2 — Determining the Graphs of Linear Inequalities. Consider $y > 4x - 6$. Its boundary line is determined by the equation of the line. Build the boundary line, decide whether it is solid or dashed, and shade the correct half-plane. Then test the point (0, 0).
hints: The boundary of y > 4x − 6 is the line with slope 4 and y-intercept −6.
> leaves the line itself out of the solutions.
Substitute (0, 0): is 0 > 4(0) − 6 true?

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. For > or <, the boundary line is…

steps.title: Boundary line
steps.instruction: The boundary line divides the plane into two half-planes; the symbol says which half-plane holds the solutions.

steps.title: Solid or dashed
steps.instruction: ≥ or ≤: solid, because points on the line are solutions. > or <: dashed, because no point on the line is.

steps.title: Test point
steps.instruction: If (0, 0) is a solution, shade its half-plane; if not, shade the other one. (Use another point if the line passes through the origin.)

solutionReview.headline: Boundary, style, shading, test.
reasoning: Boundary y = 4x − 6: plot (0, −6) and (1, −2).
> is strict, so the line is dashed.
0 > 4(0) − 6 is true, so shade the half-plane containing (0, 0): above the line.
solutionReview.commonError: Shading below because the slope is positive: the symbol decides the side, not the slope.

questions.prompt: Coach Garcia is analyzing the scoring patterns of players on his basketball team. Kai averages 20 points per game from two-point and three-point shots. Let x be the number of two-point shots and y the number of three-point shots. Coach Garcia believes the team can win the district playoffs if Kai scores AT LEAST 20 points per game. Write the inequality in the tool, then graph it: build the boundary line, choose solid or dashed, and shade the half-plane of combinations that meet the goal. Then test the point (6, 4).
directionSteps: Write the inequality for at least 20 points.
Shade the half-plane that meets the goal.
hints: "At least" means greater than or equal to.
Points that make exactly 20 points are on the boundary line, such as (10, 0) and (4, 4).
A point that meets the goal is on the side you shade.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. "At least 20" means…

steps.title: From an equation to an inequality
steps.instruction: Replace "=" with the symbol the situation needs: at least ≥, no more than ≤, more than >, fewer than <.

steps.title: Half-plane
steps.instruction: The graph of a linear inequality in two variables is a half-plane, half of the coordinate plane, on one side of a boundary line.

solutionReview.headline: Model, boundary, style, shading, test.
reasoning: At least 20 points: 2x + 3y ≥ 20.
The boundary 2x + 3y = 20 passes through (10, 0) and (4, 4); ≥ includes 20, so it is solid.
Shade above: (6, 4) gives 24 ≥ 20, so it is in the shaded half-plane.
solutionReview.commonError: Drawing a dashed line: exactly 20 points meets the goal, so the boundary is part of the solution.

questions.prompt: Complete the table of Kai’s total points for each combination of shots. Then decide where on your graph the combinations that meet or exceed her average lie.
directionSteps: Find the total for each row of the table.
Decide where the combinations that meet the average lie.

responses.label: The combinations that meet or exceed 20 points are…

hints: Total = 2 · (two-point shots) + 3 · (three-point shots).
Compare each total with 20.
The points with totals of 20 or more fall on one side of the boundary.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. The total for (8, 2) is…

solutionReview.headline: Evaluate 2x + 3y for each row.
reasoning: Totals: 11, 15, 17 (below 20) and 22, 24, 33 (20 or more).
The combinations with 20 or more points lie on or above the line 2x + 3y = 20.
solutionReview.commonError: Adding the shot counts (x + y) instead of the points.

questions.prompt: Interpret the solutions. Compare the solutions of 2x + 3y = 20 with those of 2x + 3y ≥ 20. Then decide whether (6.5, 5.5) makes sense for Kai, and find Kai’s points for a point below the line and a point on it.
directionSteps: Decide whether the decimal point makes sense in the situation.
Find the points for each of the other two combinations.
Explain what those two points mean.

responses.label: How do the solutions differ?
options: The equation’s solutions are only the points on the line; the inequality’s are the line and the half-plane above it
The inequality has fewer solutions than the equation
The equation’s solutions are the half-plane above the line
responses.answer: The equation’s solutions are only the points on the line; the inequality’s are the line and the half-plane above it

responses.label: Does (6.5, 5.5) make sense as a solution for Kai?
options: No — it satisfies the inequality, but Kai cannot make half of a shot, so only whole numbers make sense
Yes — every point in the shaded half-plane makes sense
No — it is below the line
Yes — Kai can make any number of shots
responses.answer: No — it satisfies the inequality, but Kai cannot make half of a shot, so only whole numbers make sense

responses.label: Kai’s points for 2 two-point shots and 3 three-point shots, (2, 3)
Kai’s points for 1 two-point shot and 6 three-point shots, (1, 6)
What do those two points mean?
options: (2, 3) is below the line and misses the goal; (1, 6) is on the line and meets it exactly
(2, 3) is on the line; (1, 6) is below it
Both points are above the line
responses.answer: (2, 3) is below the line and misses the goal; (1, 6) is on the line and meets it exactly

hints: An equation is true only on its line; an inequality with ≥ is true on the line and on one side of it.
Substitute each point into 2x + 3y and compare the total with Kai’s goal.
Think about what x and y count.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. The number of shots Kai makes must be…

solutionReview.headline: A solution must make the inequality true and make sense.
reasoning: 2x + 3y = 20 is true only on the line; 2x + 3y ≥ 20 is true on the line and above it.
(6.5, 5.5) gives 29.5 ≥ 20, but half a shot is impossible.
(2, 3) gives 13, less than 20 (below the line); (1, 6) gives exactly 20 (on the line).
solutionReview.answerSummary: line only vs. line and above; 29.5, but no; 13; 20
solutionReview.commonError: Accepting every point in the shaded region in a situation that counts whole things.

questions.prompt: Like linear equations, linear inequalities take different forms: ax + by < c, ax + by ≤ c, ax + by > c and ax + by ≥ c. Write each statement about Kai’s game as an inequality, where x is her two-point shots and y her three-point shots.
directionSteps: Decide what each statement counts: points or shots.
Choose the symbol each phrase describes.

responses.label: She scores no more than 30 points.
She makes fewer than 12 shots in all.
Her two-point shots outnumber her three-point shots by more than 4.

hints: "At least" and "no more than" include the number itself.
"More than" and "fewer than" leave the number out.
Points come from 2x + 3y; the number of shots is x + y.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. "No more than" includes the number itself?

solutionReview.headline: Include the number or leave it out.
reasoning: At least ≥ and no more than ≤ include the number; more than > and fewer than < leave it out.
solutionReview.commonError: Reading "no more than" as <: the number itself is allowed.

questions.prompt: Four graphs share one boundary line, y = (1/2)x − 3, through (0, −3) and (6, 0). Graph a: dashed line, the half-plane above it shaded. Graph b: solid line, the half-plane below it shaded. Graph c: dashed line, the half-plane below it shaded. Write the inequality graphs a, b and c show, and the fourth inequality with this boundary, which none of them shows.
directionSteps: Use solid or dashed to narrow the symbol.
Use the shaded side to finish each inequality.
Write the fourth inequality with this boundary.

responses.label: The inequality no graph shows (you graph it next)

hints: Dashed goes with < or >; solid with ≤ or ≥.
Solved for y, > and ≥ shade above; < and ≤ shade below.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Solved for y, y < mx + b shades…

solutionReview.headline: Line style, then side.
reasoning: a: dashed and above → y > (1/2)x − 3. b: solid and below → y ≤ (1/2)x − 3. c: dashed and below → y < (1/2)x − 3.
The one left is y ≥ (1/2)x − 3: solid and above.
solutionReview.commonError: Choosing by the line alone: all four inequalities share the same boundary line.

questions.prompt: Graph d. Graph $y \ge \frac{1}{2}x - 3$, the inequality no graph showed. Consider the symbol and which half-plane will be shaded before you test any points.
hints: Start at the y-intercept and use the slope as rise over run.
≥ includes the boundary.
Solved for y, ≥ shades above.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. A slope of 1/2 means…

solutionReview.headline: Solid line, shaded above.
reasoning: Plot (0, −3), then up 1 and right 2 to (2, −2).
≥ includes equality: solid line.
Shade above; (0, 0) gives 0 ≥ −3, true.
solutionReview.commonError: Using a rise of 2 and a run of 1 for the slope 1/2.

questions.prompt: Graph $y > x + 3$.
hints: The boundary has slope 1 and y-intercept 3.
Which symbols use a dashed line?
Test a point that is not on the line.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. For y > x + 3, the point (0, 0) is…

solutionReview.headline: Dashed line, shaded above.
reasoning: Boundary y = x + 3 through (0, 3) and (1, 4); > means dashed.
0 > 0 + 3 is false, so shade the side without (0, 0): above.
solutionReview.commonError: Shading the side with (0, 0) after the test said it was not a solution.

questions.prompt: Graph $y \le -\frac{1}{3}x + 4$.
hints: A slope of −1/3: down 1, right 3 (or up 1, left 3).
≤ includes the boundary.
Test (0, 0).

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. A slope of −1/3 means…

solutionReview.headline: Solid line, shaded below.
reasoning: Plot (0, 4), then down 1 and right 3 to (3, 3).
≤ includes equality: solid.
0 ≤ 4 is true, so shade the side with (0, 0): below.
solutionReview.commonError: Moving down 3 and right 1 for the slope −1/3.

questions.prompt: Graph $2x - y < 4$. First rewrite it with y alone in the tool — watch what happens to the symbol — then graph it.
directionSteps: Rewrite the inequality with y alone.
hints: Subtract 2x from each side first.
Dividing (or multiplying) both sides by a negative number reverses the symbol.
Check the side you shade with a test point in the original inequality.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. When you divide both sides of an inequality by −1, the symbol…

solutionReview.headline: Rewrite, reverse, graph.
reasoning: 2x − y < 4 → −y < −2x + 4 → y > 2x − 4 (dividing by −1 reverses the symbol).
Dashed line through (0, −4) and (2, 0); shade above.
Check (0, 0): 2(0) − 0 < 4 is true, and (0, 0) is above the line.
solutionReview.commonError: Keeping < after dividing by −1, which shades the wrong half-plane.

questions.prompt: Worked example — write a linear inequality for a graph. A graph has a SOLID boundary line through (0, −5) and (2, −8), and the half-plane ABOVE the line is shaded. Write the boundary’s equation pieces, choose the symbol, and check with a test point.
directionSteps: Find the slope of the boundary line.
Choose the symbol from the line style and the shaded side.
Write the inequality and check it with a test point.

responses.label: Solid line, shaded above: the symbol is
Test (0, 0): 0 ≥ −(3/2)(0) − 5 is…
options: true, and (0, 0) is in the shaded half-plane
true, so the line is dashed
responses.answer: true, and (0, 0) is in the shaded half-plane

hints: Slope = change in y ÷ change in x between the two points.
The point with x = 0 gives the y-intercept.
Solid means the boundary is included; above means y is greater.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. A solid boundary line means the points on the line are…

steps.title: Writing an inequality from a graph
steps.instruction: Write the boundary’s equation as you would for a line, then replace = with the symbol the line style and the shaded side call for. Test a point to check.

solutionReview.headline: Equation of the line, then the symbol.
reasoning: Slope = (−8 − (−5))/(2 − 0) = −3/2; the y-intercept is −5.
Solid and above: y ≥ −(3/2)x − 5.
Check (0, 0): 0 ≥ −5 is true, and (0, 0) is shaded.
solutionReview.commonError: Using > for a solid line.

questions.prompt: Write a linear inequality for graphs a, b and c. Graph a: a DASHED boundary line through (0, 2) and (1, 6); the shaded half-plane contains (0, 0). Graph b: a SOLID boundary line through (0, −3) and (6, 0); the half-plane above it is shaded. Graph c: a DASHED boundary line through (0, −2) and (4, 1); the half-plane below it is shaded.
directionSteps: Find each boundary line’s slope and y-intercept.
Choose each symbol from the line style and the shaded side.
hints: Find each slope from the two points, and read the y-intercept at x = 0.
Dashed: < or >. Solid: ≤ or ≥.
For graph a, test (0, 0): which symbol makes 0 ? 4(0) + 2 true?

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. A dashed boundary uses…

solutionReview.headline: Line first, then the symbol.
reasoning: a: slope 4, intercept 2; dashed; (0, 0) shaded and 0 < 2, so y < 4x + 2.
b: slope 1/2, intercept −3; solid, above: y ≥ (1/2)x − 3.
c: slope 3/4, intercept −2; dashed, below: y < (3/4)x − 2.
solutionReview.commonError: For a steep line, reading "to the right" as "above": test (0, 0) to be sure of the side.

questions.prompt: Activity 4.3 — Interpreting Graphs of Linear Inequalities. César has a $50 prepaid phone card. The table shows combinations of minutes for calls within the United States, x, and calls to Mexico, y, that use up the whole card. Write an inequality for the minutes he can use.

columns.label: Calls within the United States, x (minutes)

directionSteps: Find the rate of change from the table.

responses.label: Rate of change (Mexico minutes per United States minute)
Inequality for the minutes César can use
Why that symbol?
options: He can use the whole card or less of it, so the combinations are on or below the line
responses.answer: He can use the whole card or less of it, so the combinations are on or below the line

hints: Rate of change = change in y ÷ change in x between two rows.
The row with x = 0 gives the y-intercept.
He cannot spend more than the card holds.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. The card is worth $50, so he can spend…

solutionReview.headline: A line from the table, then "at most".
reasoning: (80 − 100)/(50 − 0) = −0.4, and the y-intercept is 100.
The card limits him to the line or below: y ≤ −0.4x + 100.
solutionReview.commonError: Using ≥: combinations above the line cost more than $50.

questions.prompt: Graph César’s inequality, written in standard form. Each minute within the United States costs $0.20 and each minute to Mexico costs $0.50 (250 United States minutes, or 100 Mexico minutes, use the whole $50). Enter the model in the tool — coefficients, symbol and the $50 — then build the boundary, choose solid or dashed, and shade. Then test the point (100, 80).
directionSteps: Enter the model in the tool.
Shade the half-plane of combinations he can afford.
hints: Cost of calls within the United States plus cost of calls to Mexico is at most 50.
The intercepts from the table are on the boundary.
Substitute (100, 80) into the cost.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. The cost of x minutes at $0.20 per minute is…

solutionReview.headline: Cost model, then graph.
reasoning: 0.2x + 0.5y ≤ 50: the boundary passes through (250, 0) and (0, 100) and is solid.
Shade below; (100, 80) costs 20 + 40 = $60, so it is not in the shaded region.
solutionReview.commonError: Shading above: those combinations cost more than the card holds.

questions.prompt: Interpret César’s graph. Use 0.2x + 0.5y ≤ 50, where x is minutes within the United States and y is minutes to Mexico. Answer each question and explain what each part of his graph means.
directionSteps: Find the most United States minutes left after the Mexico call.
Decide whether each pair of calls fits on the card.
Explain the meaning of points on, above and below the line.

responses.label: He talks to his aunt in Mexico for 70 minutes. The most minutes he can then talk to his cousin in New York
100 minutes to San Antonio and 80 minutes to Juárez, Mexico?
options: No — that costs $60, more than the card
No — calls to Mexico are not allowed
responses.answer: No — that costs $60, more than the card

responses.label: 55 minutes to Mexico City and 90 minutes to Denver?
options: Yes — that costs $45.50, which is at most $50
No — the point is above the line
responses.answer: Yes — that costs $45.50, which is at most $50

responses.label: Points on the line mean…
options: combinations that use exactly the whole $50
combinations that leave money on the card
responses.answer: combinations that use exactly the whole $50

responses.label: Points above the line mean…
options: combinations that leave money on the card

responses.label: Points below the line (in the first quadrant) mean…
options: combinations that leave money on the card
responses.answer: combinations that leave money on the card

hints: 70 minutes to Mexico costs 0.5 · 70 dollars; what is left pays for minutes at $0.20 each.
Find the total cost of each pair of calls and compare it with $50.
On the line the cost is exactly $50.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. 70 minutes to Mexico costs…

solutionReview.headline: Cost decides: on the line $50, above more, below less.
reasoning: On the line: exactly $50. Above: more than $50. Below: money left over.
solutionReview.commonError: Comparing total minutes with 250: the two kinds of minutes cost different amounts.

questions.prompt: Talk the Talk — There’s a Fine Line. Use the line x + y = 12. Describe how to graph each inequality. Then use the line x + y = 0: write the inequality whose solution set each description gives.
directionSteps: Describe the graph of each inequality with the line x + y = 12.
Write the inequality for each solution set with the line x + y = 0.

responses.label: x + y < 12
options: dashed line, shade below (test (0, 0): 0 < 12 is true)
responses.answer: dashed line, shade below (test (0, 0): 0 < 12 is true)

responses.label: x + y > 12
options: dashed line, shade above (test (0, 0): 0 > 12 is false)
responses.answer: dashed line, shade above (test (0, 0): 0 > 12 is false)

responses.label: The line x + y = 0 and the half-plane above it
The half-plane below the line x + y = 0, without the line
The line x + y = 0 and the half-plane below it

hints: The symbol decides solid or dashed.
The second line passes through the origin, so test a different point, such as (1, 1).
Solved for y, > and ≥ are above; < and ≤ are below.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. x + y = 0 passes through (0, 0), so to test a side use…

solutionReview.headline: Same line, different symbols.
reasoning: x + y < 12: dashed, below; x + y ≤ 12: solid, below; x + y > 12: dashed, above.
With the line x + y = 0: the line and above is x + y ≥ 0; below without the line is x + y < 0; the line and below is x + y ≤ 0.
solutionReview.commonError: Testing (0, 0) for x + y ≥ 0: the origin is on the line, so it cannot tell you which side to shade.

sections.title: Practice — Graphing and Writing Linear Inequalities

questions.prompt: Graph $y > {{m|coef}}x {{b|signed}}$. Then test the point (0, 0).
hints: Plot the y-intercept, then use the slope.
> leaves the boundary out.
Substitute (0, 0) to decide the side.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. For y > mx + b, the line is…

solutionReview.headline: Dashed line, shaded above.
reasoning: Boundary y = {{m|coef}}x {{b|signed}}: plot (0, {{b}}) and (1, {{mb}}).
> is strict: dashed. Solved for y with >, shade above.
solutionReview.commonError: Using the slope’s sign to pick the side.

questions.prompt: Graph $y \le {{sg|coef}}\frac{ {{pa}} }{ {{q}} }x {{b|signed}}$.
hints: From the y-intercept, rise by the numerator and run by the denominator.
≤ includes the boundary.
Solved for y, ≤ shades below.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. A slope of p/q means…

solutionReview.headline: Solid line, shaded below.
reasoning: Plot (0, {{b}}), then use a rise of {{p}} and a run of {{q}} to reach ({{q}}, {{bp}}).
≤ includes equality: solid; shade below.
solutionReview.commonError: Swapping the rise and the run.

questions.prompt: Graph $ {{A}}x - y < {{C}} $. Rewrite it with y alone in the tool first.
directionSteps: Rewrite the inequality with y alone.
hints: Subtract the x-term from both sides first.
Dividing by a negative number reverses the symbol.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. −y < 6 becomes…

solutionReview.headline: Rewrite, reverse, graph.
reasoning: {{A}}x − y < {{C}} → −y < −{{A}}x {{C|signed}} → y > {{A}}x {{nC|signed}} (dividing by −1 reverses the symbol).
Dashed line, shaded above.
solutionReview.commonError: Forgetting to reverse the symbol.

questions.prompt: A club sells muffins for ${{p}} each and smoothies for ${{q}} each. It needs to raise at least ${{T}}. Let x be the number of muffins and y the number of smoothies. Write the inequality, then check one plan: {{x0}} muffins and {{y0}} smoothies.
directionSteps: Find the money the plan raises.
Find how much more than the goal it raises.

responses.label: Money raised by {{x0}} muffins and {{y0}} smoothies ($)
How many dollars over the goal is that?

hints: Money from muffins plus money from smoothies is at least the goal.
Multiply each count by its price, then add.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. "At least" means…

solutionReview.headline: Price times count, then "at least".
reasoning: {{p}}({{x0}}) + {{q}}({{y0}}) = {{R}}, which is {{E}} over the goal.
solutionReview.commonError: Using ≤ for "at least".

questions.prompt: Which point is a solution of $ {{A}}x + {{B}}y \le {{C}} $? Substitute each point.
directionSteps: Decide which point makes the inequality true.
hints: Substitute x and y, then compare the value with the constant.
≤ is true when the value is less than or equal to the constant.

solutionReview.headline: Substitute and compare.
reasoning: Only ({{xa}}, {{ya}}) is at most {{C}}.
solutionReview.commonError: Reversing the comparison.

questions.prompt: Vertical and horizontal boundaries. Write an inequality for graphs a and b. Graph a: a dashed vertical line x = 3, the half-plane to its left shaded. Graph b: a solid horizontal line y = −2, the half-plane above it shaded.
directionSteps: Use the line and its style to choose the symbol.
hints: A vertical line x = c: left means x is less than c.
A horizontal line y = c: above means y is greater than c.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Points to the left of x = 3 have x-coordinates…

solutionReview.headline: Vertical: compare x. Horizontal: compare y.
reasoning: Left of the dashed line x = 3: x < 3.
Above the solid line y = −2: y ≥ −2.
solutionReview.commonError: Writing y < 3 for a vertical boundary.

questions.prompt: Graph $x \ge -2$ in the coordinate plane.
hints: x = −2 is a vertical line: use the vertical-line method.
≥ includes the line.
Points to the right have larger x-coordinates.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. The graph of x = −2 in the plane is…

solutionReview.headline: Solid vertical line, shaded right.
reasoning: Boundary x = −2 (vertical), solid because ≥.
Shade to the right, where x ≥ −2.
solutionReview.commonError: Drawing a horizontal line y = −2.

solutionReview.headline: Words to symbols.
solutionReview.commonError: Writing y − 2x for "twice the first minus the second".

questions.prompt: A food truck sells tacos for $3 and burritos for $8. The owner wants to take in at least $240 today. Let x be the number of tacos and y the number of burritos. Enter the model in the tool, graph it, and test the point (40, 20).

Shade the half-plane that meets the goal.

The intercepts (80, 0) and (0, 30) are on the boundary.

solutionReview.headline: Model, graph, test.
reasoning: 3x + 8y ≥ 240; boundary through (80, 0) and (0, 30), solid.
Shade above; (40, 20) gives 280 ≥ 240, so it meets the goal.
solutionReview.commonError: Shading below the line, where the money is less than $240.

questions.prompt: Error analysis. Marcus graphed y < −2x + 1 with a SOLID boundary line and shaded the half-plane below it. Write the inequality his graph actually shows, identify his error, and check his shading with the point (0, 0).
directionSteps: Write the inequality Marcus’s graph shows.
Decide which part of the graph is wrong.
Check the shading with the test point.

responses.label: Marcus’s error:
options: The line should be dashed, because < does not include the boundary
The shading should be above the line
responses.answer: The line should be dashed, because < does not include the boundary

responses.label: Test (0, 0): 0 < −2(0) + 1 is…
options: true, so the shading below (with the origin) is correct
false, so the shading is wrong
true, so the line is solid
responses.answer: true, so the shading below (with the origin) is correct

hints: A solid line shaded below shows ≤.
Check the line style against the symbol.
Check the side with a test point.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. For <, the boundary is…

solutionReview.headline: Check style, then side.
reasoning: A solid line shaded below shows y ≤ −2x + 1, which includes the line.
< is strict, so the boundary must be dashed.
(0, 0): 0 < 1 is true and the origin is below the line, so the shading is right.
solutionReview.answerSummary: y ≤ −2x + 1; the line should be dashed

questions.prompt: Which points are solutions of 4x − 2y ≤ 8? Find 4x − 2y at each point, then decide.
directionSteps: Decide which point is not a solution.
Decide which point is on the boundary line.

responses.label: Which point is NOT a solution?
Which point is on the boundary line?

hints: Substitute x and y, then compare the value with the right side.
A point that makes the two sides equal is on the solid boundary — and ≤ includes it.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. At (1, 1), 4x − 2y equals…

solutionReview.answerSummary: 0, 10, 8, 6; (3, 1) is not a solution; (2, 0) is on the line

questions.prompt: A boundary line passes through (0, 4) and (2, 0). It is solid, and (0, 0) is NOT in the shaded half-plane. Write the inequality.
directionSteps: Use the test point to choose the side.
hints: Find the slope from the two points; the y-intercept is where x = 0.
(0, 0) is not shaded, so the inequality is false at (0, 0).
Solid: ≤ or ≥.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Is 0 ≤ −2(0) + 4 true?

solutionReview.headline: Line, then the side without the origin.
reasoning: Slope −2, y-intercept 4: y = −2x + 4.
0 ≤ 4 is true, but (0, 0) is not shaded, so the symbol is ≥: y ≥ −2x + 4.
solutionReview.commonError: Choosing ≤ because the origin is "below": the origin must be excluded.
